01 -- Project Overview

An all-in-one solution
for vital monitoring.

The Medical Watch Project is a functional prototype of a medical-alert wearable developed at George Mason University. The system monitors key vitals including body temperature, heart rate, SpO2, fall detection, and GPS location, transmitting data continuously to AWS IoT Core via MQTT and visualizing it through a real-time caregiver web dashboard.

The current deliverables include a working breadboard-based prototype with a validated sensor suite and FreeRTOS firmware, a functional cloud backend and guardian web UI, and a 3D-modeled enclosure design. The breadboard form factor was used for prototyping and validation. A custom PCB would be required to bring the electronics to wearable size.

The project addresses a real gap between consumer smartwatches, which are not FDA-cleared and do not auto-alert emergency services, and traditional medical alert devices like Life Alert, which require a conscious user to press a button. This system is designed to work even when the patient cannot act.

Wearable Device

Wi-Fi-enabled wearable with full sensor suite continuously aggregating vital health metrics and environmental data.

AWS IoT Cloud Infrastructure

Secure MQTT transmission to AWS IoT Core with DynamoDB storage, Lambda processing, and Cognito authentication.

Predictive AI Model

Lightweight AI on AWS analyzes the continuous data stream to detect anomalies and identify potential emergencies in real time.

Guardian Web Dashboard

AWS triggers immediate alerts and streams real-time vitals, location, and health data to caregivers and first responders.

02 -- System Architecture

End-to-end data flow.

The system operates across three layers: the wearable device, the AWS cloud backend, and the guardian interface. Data flows from the patient's wrist to first responders in seconds.

04 -- Hardware Design

Sensor suite and microcontroller.

The core hardware platform is built around a dual-core ESP32 (ESP32-D0WDQ6), selected for its multi-threading capabilities and peripheral support, requiring a minimum of two I2C buses and one UART interface to communicate with the full onboard sensor suite.

Heart Rate and SpO2

MAX30102

Isolated on Core 1 with its own dedicated I2C bus (Wire1). A dual-state machine alternates between a 50-second heart rate window and a 10-second SpO2 window, cycling at approximately 50 Hz with zero I2C bus contention.

Body Temperature

MAX30205

Clinical-grade thermometry meeting ASTM E1112 specifications. Sampled at 2 Hz at I2C address 0x48. Outlier rejection filters readings outside the 25 to 50 degrees Celsius range, followed by a 10-sample moving average filter.

Fall Detection

MPU6050

6-axis IMU sampled at 500 Hz with an accelerometer range of plus or minus 8g. A three-stage algorithm detects free fall below 4.9 m/s squared, then an impact spike above 9.8 m/s squared within 300ms, then confirms via 2 seconds of inactivity to eliminate false positives.

GPS Location

NEO-6M

Standalone GNSS module on UART2 (GPIO 16 and 17) at 9600 baud. Provides atomic UTC timestamps directly from satellite data plus 2D/3D positional fixes with HDOP accuracy reporting. Indoor fallback sets gpsHasFix to false to prevent corrupt coordinates.

Environmental Sensor

BMP280

Barometric pressure, ambient temperature, and relative altitude sampled at 1 Hz. Configured with FILTER_X16 to suppress wind-induced pressure spikes. Altitude is computed against a 1013.25 hPa sea-level baseline.

Wear Detection

ESP32 Touch Pins

Dual capacitive pins on GPIO 12 and 14, sampled at 10 Hz. Both pins must simultaneously drop below a threshold of 200 to confirm a true worn state. If either pin loses contact, the isWorn flag updates immediately so the cloud reflects accurate device status.

FREERTOS DUAL-CORE TASK ARCHITECTURE -- ESP32-D0WDQ6

ESP32 + FreeRTOS Dual-Core Architecture

The firmware uses FreeRTOS to unlock true hardware parallelism across both cores of the ESP32, isolating high-frequency biometric sampling completely from Wi-Fi and MQTT network overhead. This ensures that SpO2 and heart rate readings are never delayed by a cloud handshake, and a fall event is never missed because the network task was holding the processor.

The firmware was developed in Arduino IDE using C++, with FreeRTOS enabling deterministic, multi-threaded task scheduling. Sensor data is written to thread-safe global variables shared in volatile memory, then consumed by the background AWS sync task.

  • CORE 0 -- HIGH
    Sensor Combo Task

    MPU6050 fall detection at 500 Hz, MAX30205 body temperature at 2 Hz, BMP280 environmental at 1 Hz, NEO-6M GPS via UART, and capacitive touch wear detection at 10 Hz, all running on the primary I2C bus concurrently.

  • CORE 1 -- MED
    MAX30102 Biometric Task

    Exclusively on the secondary I2C bus. Alternates between collecting raw Red and IR PPG arrays for SpO2 and capturing peak-to-peak deltas for heart rate averages, isolated from I2C clock collisions with Core 0 sensors.

  • CORE 1 -- LOW
    AWS Sync Task

    Manages Wi-Fi, TLS/SSL certificates, and MQTT client keep-alives. Reads thread-safe global variables, serializes them into a JSON payload, and publishes to AWS IoT Core every 5 seconds without introducing latency into the vital-sign extraction routines.

05 -- Firmware and Cloud

Data pipeline and telemetry payload.

Every 5 seconds the device serializes a structured JSON telemetry payload and publishes to AWS IoT Core via MQTT over TLS. AWS Lambda functions handle normalization, anomaly detection, and alert routing to the guardian dashboard.

06 -- Market Research and I-Corps

Bridging the gap in
medical alert technology.

Through the NSF I-Corps program at the Mason MIX (August 2025 Cohort), our team conducted over 20 customer discovery interviews with nurses, elderly care physicians, the Fairfax County Department of Family Services, and contacts at IBM and Microsoft. We also attended the World Quantum Congress at Tysons Corner. Mason had just joined the NSF Mid-South Region Hub, giving us direct access to I-Corps instructors, industry experts, and tech transfer professionals.

Consumer Smartwatches

Apple, Samsung, and Fitbit dominate the wearable space but are not FDA-cleared for medical diagnosis, do not automatically alert emergency services, and are too expensive for facilities to deploy per resident at scale. They also have no mechanism to act when the wearer is unresponsive.

Traditional Medical Alert Devices

Systems like Life Alert do contact emergency services and guardians but require the wearer to manually press a button. They are ineffective when a patient is unconscious or incapacitated, and they transmit no real-time medical data, leaving responders without critical context when they arrive.

Our Position: The Gap Between Both Markets

The Medical Watch Project sits between these two categories. It is designed as a low-cost, bulk-deployable system that automatically tracks vital data and dispatches alerts to EMS and caregivers without requiring any action from the wearer. Hospitals, government agencies, and care facilities can purchase and deploy it at scale.

Customer Discovery Takeaways

The elder care industry is more deregulated than most people assume. Government oversight of care homes often depends entirely on residents filing their own complaints, and due to the social dynamics inside these facilities, residents are frequently hesitant or afraid to speak up. Many facilities are also severely understaffed, and we heard allegations of facilities disabling in-room call buttons in certain patients' rooms to keep compliance numbers clean.

  • Strong demand from nursing staff. The device acts as an extra set of eyes, letting overworked staff prioritize patients who need immediate attention rather than performing manual checks on every resident.

  • Institutional transparency as a selling point. Real-time data gives facilities a concrete way to demonstrate accountability to families, reducing constant check-in calls and replacing invasive manual supervision.

  • Resident autonomy. Patients who previously required constant, invasive supervision can regain independence, knowing the watch will automatically call for help the moment a medical emergency occurs.

  • Family peace of mind. Loved ones gain direct access to health data and treatment insights without needing to cross-examine facility staff for basic information.

07 -- Project Summary

Deliverables, outcomes,
and future considerations.

The following documents the project outcomes -- what was delivered, what the known technical limitations are, and what future engineering work would be required to bring this to a production-ready medical device.

Completed Deliverables

01
Complete

Working Breadboard Prototype

A fully functional breadboard-based prototype integrating all six sensors -- MAX30102, MAX30205, MPU6050, NEO-6M, BMP280, and capacitive touch pins -- running concurrently on FreeRTOS across both ESP32 cores. Fall detection, wear detection, and real-time vitals acquisition are all validated and operational.

02
Complete

Functional Cloud Backend and Guardian UI

A complete AWS backend built on IoT Core, Lambda, DynamoDB, Cognito, and S3. The prototype transmits a live JSON telemetry payload every 5 seconds via MQTT over TLS. A guardian web application provides real-time visualization of vitals, location, and device status. A full system walkthrough video and UI screenshots are included in the section below.

03
Complete

Enclosure Design

A 3D-modeled enclosure designed in Onshape and optimized for FDM 3D printing. The pill-shaped form factor is sized for tricep-mounting with a back-face sensor window, wireless charging coils, and epoxy sealing for waterproofing. The enclosure is finalized in CAD -- hardware miniaturization via PCB is the remaining step to fit the electronics inside.

Known Limitations and Open Engineering Problems

A
Known Limitation

Breadboard Form Factor

The prototype is breadboard-based and does not fit inside the designed enclosure. A custom PCB would be required to bring the hardware to wearable size. This is the primary gap between the current prototype and a deployable device.

B
Known Limitation

Wireless Charging

Wireless charging coils are incorporated into the enclosure design but were not implemented in the prototype hardware. This would be addressed during a PCB design phase.

C
Known Limitation

AI Anomaly Detection

The AWS Lambda and data pipeline infrastructure is in place to support a predictive model. The anomaly detection model itself remains early stage -- a production implementation would integrate AWS SageMaker in a future development phase.

Future Work

1
Future Work

Custom PCB Design and Manufacturing

A custom PCB would consolidate the breadboard components into a footprint small enough to fit the enclosure, enabling a true wearable form factor with integrated wireless charging.

2
Future Work

Pilot Testing and Clinical Validation

A production-ready version would require structured clinical testing, sensor accuracy validation against medical-grade devices, and a pathway toward FDA clearance.

cloud-connected monitoring system.

Technical Implementation

Embedded Systems and Device Connectivity

The ESP32 was selected and configured as the main controller for its Wi-Fi and Bluetooth capabilities and Arduino compatibility. It serves as the foundation for all sensor data collection and cloud transmission.

The device-to-cloud connection works as follows: the ESP32 publishes all sensor data over MQTT to AWS IoT Core, which then writes each reading automatically into the VitalsReadings DynamoDB table. The connection has been fully validated -- the ESP32 connects to AWS and transmits live sensor data successfully. A second ESP32 running the full sensor system was also integrated as an additional device in IoT Core, confirming that multiple devices can flow data into the same DynamoDB backend simultaneously.

AWS IoT Core to DynamoDB Pipeline

An AWS IoT rule was configured to write incoming MQTT messages straight into DynamoDB as they arrive, with no manual handling in between. One key implementation detail discovered during setup: when configuring the IoT rule, the "Write message data to this column" field must be left empty so the entire JSON message is inserted as an attribute rather than being dropped. This took non-trivial debugging to identify.

CloudWatch dashboards were set up to monitor the pipeline and verify data is flowing as expected. AWS HIPAA compliance documentation was also reviewed to understand requirements for processing and storing protected health information, which informed the authentication and access control decisions made downstream.

DynamoDB Data Modeling and Query Optimization

The data is modeled using a partition/sort key (pk/sk) structure so readings are organized per patient and per device. The system moved away from scanning the entire table on every request -- readings are now queried by patient ID, which pulls a patient's vitals history directly and efficiently. This patient-scoped, time-ordered query approach supports 24-hour vitals views, trend analysis over time, and future doctor dashboards and alerting without degrading performance at scale.

The backend uses three active DynamoDB tables: Doctors, Patients, and VitalsReadings.

Serverless API -- Lambda and API Gateway

To make stored vitals available to the web app, a serverless backend was built using AWS Lambda functions behind API Gateway. Two Lambda functions were built and deployed: getPatients and getPatientReadings, both running on Node.js. They read patient and vitals data from DynamoDB and return it as JSON over REST endpoints, so the frontend never talks to the database directly. The live API Gateway endpoint returns patient readings including the latest reading and full reading history.

Secure Authentication -- AWS Cognito

The original web app had only a placeholder login screen that collected a username and moved to the next page without verifying anything -- there was no real authentication. This was replaced with a full, secure sign-in flow backed by AWS Cognito.

AWS Cognito was integrated as the identity provider, with a Cognito user pool configured and wired into the app through an OIDC authentication provider so login is handled by AWS rather than custom code. The login page now redirects users to authenticate against Cognito and handles the sign-in callback. Protected routes were built so the dashboard and individual patient pages can only be reached by authenticated users -- anyone not signed in is automatically redirected to the login page. Session-based login persists an authenticated user's session appropriately across the app.

This authentication layer directly supports the HIPAA access-control requirements researched earlier, since patient vitals are no longer reachable without a verified login.

Web Application -- Ionic + React + TypeScript

The AWS pipeline was integrated into the team's existing web application, an Ionic and React TypeScript dashboard. The frontend consumes the deployed API Gateway REST routes to list patients and fetch a given patient's readings. The patient monitoring page polls AWS every 5 seconds to retrieve the newest readings and refresh the display, giving caregivers a near-real-time view of patient vitals.

The live monitoring view shows heart rate, SpO2, body temperature, and safety status (fall and worn state) as live cards, a vitals trend chart built with Recharts, GPS location displayed on a Leaflet map, and a scrolling reading history. The patient dashboard landing view lists all patients retrieved from AWS, with loading and error states handled throughout.

09 -- Enclosure and Power

Designed for real-world wear.

The enclosure was designed in Onshape and manufactured via FDM 3D printing across multiple iterations, producing a form factor representative of the target wearable device. The physical enclosure is a mockup and does not contain the prototype electronics -- fitting the full breadboard hardware inside would require a custom PCB.

Enclosure mockup worn on arm -- demonstrates target form factor

Enclosure iterations -- three printed versions showing design progression

CAD Model -- 360 Degree Rotation -- Onshape

CAD Teardown -- Internal Component Layout -- Onshape

Ergonomics

Tricep-mounted form factor, dimensioned for comfort and stability during continuous daily wear with integrated loops for an adjustable cloth strap.

Waterproofing

The design specifies epoxy sealing over any exposed gaps, including the sensor window opening on the back face. This approach is low-cost and effective without requiring custom gaskets or overmolding.

Wireless Charging

The target design uses wireless charging coils with no exposed ports, keeping the outer shell fully sealed. Wireless charging was not implemented in the breadboard prototype. Integration would occur alongside a custom PCB development phase.

Sensor Window

The MAX30102 heart rate and SpO2 sensor is positioned against the back face of the enclosure, which contacts the skin during wear. The sensor window opening is sealed with epoxy to maintain waterproofing while still allowing optical contact with the skin.

Power System

3.7V 2000mAh LiPo battery charged via TP4056 CC/CV module. XL6009 boost converter provides a stable 5V rail to the ESP32, while all sensors run from the ESP32 onboard 3.3V regulated supply pin.
